Making protein language models fine-tuning and sharing accessible to all - no coding or advanced machine learning expertise required! **Access via [ColabSaprot](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/SaprotHub_v2.ipynb?hl=en) (35M,650M), [ColabSeprot](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ColabSeprot.ipynb?hl=en) (including ColabESM1b (650M), ColabESM2 (35M, 150M, 650M), ColabProTrek (35M, 650M), ColabProtBERT (420M)), [ColabESMC](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-VC.ipynb) (300M,600M), and [ColabESM3](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-V3.ipynb) (1.4B) ！** Note that ColabSaprot and ColabESM3 also supports training and prediction using only amino acid sequences. Watch [the ColabSaprot video tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nmLtjlCI_7M&t=716s). Go to [the OPMC website](https://theopmc.github.io/). Successful [wet-lab results](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZcDl0XYksTcUEaCfPI0tuEVo5CA031dg/view) by ColabSaprot from community. Finding models through [SaprotHub Search](https://huggingface.co/spaces/SaProtHub/SaprotHub-search), sharing your models via ColabSaprot to boost visibility and citations. ## News - **2026/01/28:** We are delighted to announce that [ColabESM3](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-V3.ipynb) and [ColabESMC](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-VC.ipynb) are now ready for use. - **2025/10/24:** ColabSaprot and SaprotHub are published in Nature Biotechnology, see [here](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-025-02859-7). - **2025/05/06:** We are delighted to announce that [ColabSeprot](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ColabSeprot.ipynb?hl=en) and [SeprotHub](https://huggingface.co/SeprotHub) are now ready for use. ColabSeprot offers access to several state-of-the-art sequence-only Protein Language Models (PLMs), including ESM1b, ESM2, ProTrek, and ProtBert, enabling streamlined fine-tuning and prediction for protein sequence analysis. - **2025/01/01:** We are delighted to announce that [ColabSaprot v2](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/SaprotHub_v2.ipynb?hl=en) (**New!!**) and [SaprotHub](https://huggingface.co/SaProtHub) are now ready for use. [Note ColabSaprot [v1](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/SaprotHub.ipynb) will no longer be updated.] Check out the [video tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nmLtjlCI_7M&t=5s) and [document](https://github.com/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/wiki/SaprotHub-v2-(latest)#a-simple-way-to-handle-unexpected-issues). ## Discussion Groups ### Slack 2025/03/21: We’ve just set up a slack group for discussing ColabSaprot or asking any questions, you can join [here](https://westlakeai.slack.com/archives/C08JNBN40P7)! ### WeChat 2024/12/01: You can scan the QR code to join our wechat groups （We currently host 5 active weichat groups with a total membership of over 1000 researchers and practitioners）: > We have 2 PhD positions for international students at Westlake University! see [here](https://x.com/duguyuan/status/1897101692665258245). ## Deploy ColabSaprot on local server (for linux os and Windows) For users who want to deploy ColabSaprot on their local server, please refer to [here](https://github.com/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/local_server). ### PLM members of OPMC - [ColabSaprot](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/SaprotHub_v2.ipynb?hl=en) (AA+3Di) - [ColabSeprot](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ColabSeprot.ipynb?hl=en) (AA) (including ColabESM1b, ColabESM2, ColabProtBert, ColabProTrek) - [ColabESMC](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-VC.ipynb) (300M,600M) - [ColabESM3](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ESM-Play-V3.ipynb) （1.4B, structure-aware） - [ColabProtT5](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ColabProtT5.ipynb) (AA) - [ColabProSST](https://colab.research.google.com/github/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/colab/ColabProSST.ipynb) (AA+structure tokens) - [SaProt-T/O](http://113.45.254.183:9527/) (edit protein based on partial sequence/structure and text, Support multiple site mutations) - [ColabMETL](https://github.com/gitter-lab/metl?tab=readme-ov-file#mutational-effect-transfer-learning) - [Evolla](http://www.chat-protein.com/) (80B protein ChatGPT) - [Pinal](http://www.denovo-pinal.com/) (16B natual language-based protein design) - [ProTrek](http://www.search-protrek.com/) (billion-scale protein search tool) ## Open Protein Modeling Consortium (OPMC) The Open Protein Modeling Consortium (OPMC) is a collaborative initiative aimed at bringing together the efforts of the protein research community. Its mission is to foster the sharing and co-development of resources, with an emphasis on individually trained decentralized models, helping to advance protein modeling through collective contributions. OPMC provides platforms/tools that support diverse protein prediction tasks, striving to make advanced protein modeling more accessible to researchers, regardless of their level of expertise in machine learning. visit our OPMC website [here](https://theopmc.github.io/) ## FAQs ### Q1: It seems like OPMC and SaprotHub are intertwined but not exactly the same. Yes, OPMC is a grand goal, and in this paper, it is primarily presented as a concept and vision. The paper introduces OPMC and implements SaprotHub as a pioneering example to drive the initial realization of OPMC. Achieving a broader implementation of OPMC requires continuous efforts from the entire community. Our OPMC members are now building other ColabPLMs, including ColabESM1b, ColabESM2, ColabProtBert, ColabT5, ColabProTrek, etc. ### Q2: I'm very interested in the OPMC side of this project? Would I be able to support OMPC independently? Yes, you can. OPMC is not tied exclusively to SaprotHub. SaprotHub serves as an initial implementation case within the broader OPMC concept. We also welcome the inclusion of new protein models in OPMC. There are generally two ways to contribute: either independently of SaprotHub, such as building ESMHub or ProtTransHub, or by joining SaprotHub. While SaprotHub is named after its first model, Saprot, it is not limited to Saprot alone and welcomes the inclusion of other language models. The concept of OPMC originated from the SaprotHub paper, so if you would like your protein model to be part of OPMC or if you adopt the similar construction approach of SaprotHub, we encourage you to cite the source paper. Also see Q9. ### Q3: What's the relation between OPMC and the OpenFold Consortium? The goal of the OpenFold Consortium is to develop free and open-source software tools. This differs from the goals of OPMC. OPMC aims to make it easy for all biologists (especially those without machine learning backgrounds and coding skills) to train their own protein models, and to share these models with the community members, allowing for integration and collaborative development on top of the existing community models. Additionally, so far, the OpenFold Consortium seems to be focusing more on protein structure prediction, while OPMC is more focused on protein function prediction. Furthermore, the number of protein function task categories is far greater than the number of structure tasks. As a result, biologists often have to fine-tune large pre-trained protein models based on their own training data, which is a key feature of OPMC. ### Q4: Is the idea to create a company that provides the resources for biologists to do model training? I'm unsure the vision here, since a lot of model training is resource and data constrained. It would be hard to create something where "every biologist to train their own AI models with just a few clicks." Who would provide the resources in this case? No, the primary motivation behind OPMC is to enable biologists to participate in protein model training and collaborative development, without direct involvement of creating a company or commercial operation. Currently, we do not provide free training resources. Users have the option to purchase GPUs, such as the A100, on platforms like Colab. OPMC primarily supports fine-tuning tasks or direct prediction tasks for protein language models, rather than pre-training. These tasks typically do not require excessively expensive computational power. With a budget of around $10, one can easily complete training and prediction tasks on several thousand samples. This cost is manageable for most individuals and academic institutions. There are also free GPU resources in Colab but they may not be sufficient for some of your tasks. In the future, we may explore options such as applying for funding or accepting donations to provide some free computational resources to users. Please note that the purpose of SaprotHub and OPMC is not to provide free computational resources. ### Q5: We are open sourcing models as well, so it would be interesting to collaborate once we release these models. However, it seems like currently the hub is geared towards SaProt as the main model of choice. Saprot is the first model to join the hub, so we named it SaprotHub. However, SaprotHub can also accept other protein models, such as ESM. Of course, you can also independently develop your own model hub. In the future, we will create a webpage for OPMC that will include all the participating models. The reason we adopted the Saprot model is that it is a near-universal model, capable of supporting any protein and residue-level prediction task, including regression, classification, ranking, as well as zero-shot mutational effect prediction and sequence design tasks. Saprot is also the state-of-the-art protein language model in the community. Additionally, we also hope to include as many other protein language models as possible, but due to limited human resources, we are unable to integrate all the existing protein language models. This is precisely the purpose of building a community (the development of ColabSaprot took us approximately 4 months. Of course, with the open-sourcing of ColabSaprot, it will be much easier to implement similar functionality for other protein language models). We believe that with the joint efforts of the entire community, the OPMC community store can become more diverse, and biologists can choose the models that best suit their needs. Therefore, we sincerely invite researchers who are interested in OPMC to join us, and if you have better suggestions, we welcome you to join us in co-building OPMC. ### Q6: ESM, AlphaFold, and Openfold models are not mentioned in the hub. OPMC mainly focuses on protein function prediction. So ESM is a good fit, AlphaFold and OpenFold target at protein structure prediction, and could be independent of OPMC or SaprotHub. But please note that developing another ColabESM will also take some time, and we welcome researchers to integrate the ESM or other models onto the hub. ### Q7: How do you foresee collaborating and sharing other open models? The SaprotHub paper primarily focuses on collaboration and sharing within the framework of one backbone model, as this can greatly reduce storage and communication costs by leveraging Adapter technique – users just need to operate on the adapters rather than the large backbone model. Since these models are based on the same backbone network, the input format, network and parameter interfaces are more consistent, which serves as the basic for community sharing, collaboration and co-construction. As for sharing between different backbone models, this remains a challenge at the moment, although it is an interesting research direction without an ideal solution yet. For example, if users want to collaborate between ESM15B and Saprot650M, they would need to upload and download the two complete models, significantly increasing communication and maintenance costs. As the number of models integrated increases, the demand on GPU performance would also increase rapidly. However, by using the same backbone model and the Adapter mechanism, these difficulties can be elegantly solved. The Adapters in SaprotHub is just like grafting techniques in biology. Just as a single tree can bear different kinds of fruit, Saprot acts like the trunk, and the adapters for various downstream tasks resemble the different fruits on the Saprot tree. Additionally, due to the differences in model architecture, input, and output across different models, it is difficult to design a unified interface. Therefore, this paper serves as an initial exploration of OPMC and does not cover collaboration between different backbone models. This may require more effort from the community, but holds promise for the future. ### Q8: How does this differentiate SaprotHub from Hugging Face? SaprotHub primarily focuses on storing lightweight Adapters, whereas Hugging Face stores complete pre-trained models. SaprotHub adopts the Adapter mechanism, which enables biologists to easily share, co-develop, and collaborate within ColabSaprot. The goal of SaprotHub is to allow all biologists to train their own protein models even without machine learning and coding background, while Hugging Face's objective is to open-source the model weights without considering the easy training aspect. SaprotHub is dedicated to establishing the AI model community for proteins, while Hugging Face has a broader scope. Therefore, SaprotHub's Adapter store can be built on top of Hugging Face or developed independently. ### Q9: If I develop other protein language models (PLMs) and online platforms following SaprotHub and ColabSaprot, can I be an author on the SaprotHub paper? All OPMC members will be listed as authors in the SaprotHub paper before its final revision, which is expected to take 4-12 months. Author's name will be included in the paper. Please note that eligibility to become an OPMC regular member is determined by the steering committee. If an OPMC author is primarily granted authorship recognition for developing other PLMHubs, they are required to acknowledge that this model automatically becomes part of the OPMC framework. In case they publish a paper, they should menton this somewhere in the paper. Researchers using this new PLMHub should also cite the original OPMC literature. ### Q10: How to be a member of OPMC or an author of SaprotHub. Before the final revision of SaprotHub, all OPMC members will be automatically included as authors. However, after the publication of SaprotHub, individuals can still join OPMC but will not be able to be listed as authors in the paper, as it is subject to the requirements of the journal publication - the final version needs to determine the author list. Regarding how to join OPMC, please refer to: [here](https://github.com/westlake-repl/SaprotHub/blob/main/Figure/OPMC.jpg). All in all, if you can come up with some cool ideas or novel ways to enhance the impact and influence of Saprot, ColabSaprot, SaprotHub, or OPMC, you may have the opportunity to be listed as an author. ### Q11: If I have made a lot of valuable contributions to OPMC, can I become an OPMC member together with my supervisor? Yes. If you have made significant valuable contributions to OPMC, it is possible to become an OPMC member alongside your PhD/postgraduate or internship supervisor. However, the acceptance of your contributions and membership status will be determined by the steering committee. Generally, in such cases, you would need to demonstrate more substantial contributions compared to regular OPMC members. You need to provide official documentation of your relationship with your supervisor, such as an official letter or document confirming their role and support. ## Citation If you find SaprotHub useful for your research, please consider citing the following paper: ``` @article{su2025democratizing, title={Democratizing protein language model training, sharing and collaboration}, author={Su, Jin and Li, Zhikai and Tao, Tianli and Han, Chenchen and He, Yan and Dai, Fengyuan and Yuan, Qingyan and Gao, Yuan and Si, Tong and Zhang, Xuting and others}, journal={Nature Biotechnology}, pages={1--7}, year={2025}, publisher={Nature Publishing Group US New York} } ``` ## Other resources - [Evolla](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.01.05.630192v1) and its [online server](http://www.chat-protein.com/) - [ProTrek](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.05.30.596740v2) and its [online server](http://search-protrek.com/) - [Pinal](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.08.01.606258v2) and its [online server](http://www.denovo-pinal.com/)

one_liner: BioBB 是生物分子模拟工具（含 MD、对接、构象分析等）的 Python 封装库，为蛋白质结构计算提供可复用的工作流组件，但本身不实现新方法，偏工程化集成。
card:
## 是什么
BioExcel Building Blocks (BioBB) 是一个基于 Python 的库，提供对常见生物分子模拟工具（如 AMBER、GROMACS、HADDOCK 等）的可移植封装（wrappers），旨在提高工具间的互操作性、简化工作流实现，并增强生物分子模拟工作流的可重用性和可复现性。它不是一个单一的模拟引擎，而是一个模块化的工作流构建框架。

## 亮点
- **模块化封装**：将不同生物分子模拟工具封装为统一的“building blocks”，每个模块对应特定工具或功能类别（如 biobb_amber 用于 AMBER MD，biobb_vs 用于虚拟筛选）。
- **高度可互操作**：通过标准化的输入/输出（如 PDB、轨迹文件）和命令行接口，实现不同工具间的无缝衔接。
- **多工作流支持**：提供对 CWL、Galaxy、PyCOMPSs 和 Jupyter Notebook 的适配器，支持多种工作流管理系统。
- **FAIR 原则**：遵循 FAIR 软件实践，提供文档、OpenAPI、Swagger 和生物信息学标准注册（如 bio.tools、WorkflowHub）。
- **丰富的演示工作流**：提供基于 Jupyter Notebook 的交互式演示，便于学习和复现。

## 为何对本课题有用
BioBB 直接覆盖蛋白质结构 × AI/计算模拟课题中的多个关键环节：
- **MD 模拟**：通过 biobb_amber、biobb_gromacs 等模块，可搭建从结构准备到 MD 模拟的完整流程，用于构象采样和动态分析。
- **构象转换与柔性分析**：biobb_flexdyn、biobb_flexserv、biobb_godmd 提供蛋白质构象景观和构象转变的计算，与构象生成/采样直接相关。
- **分子对接**：biobb_haddock 支持信息驱动的柔性蛋白-蛋白对接，可用于蛋白-蛋白互作预测。
- **结构建模与修复**：biobb_model 提供结构检查、突变和缺失原子重建，可作为 AI 预测结构（如 AlphaFold 输出）的后处理工具。
- **虚拟筛选**：biobb_vs 支持小分子虚拟筛选，可扩展至蛋白-配体对接。
- **数据获取**：biobb_io 提供从公共数据库获取结构数据的接口，便于构建训练/测试数据集。

## 怎么用
- **主入口**：BioBB 是一个 Python 库，无单一主程序；通过安装各子模块（如 `pip install biobb_amber`）并调用其 Python API 或命令行工具。
- **安装**：通过 PyPI 或 BioConda 安装，依赖见各子模块的 setup.py（如 biobb_common 是基础依赖）。
- **输入/输出**：主要处理 PDB 结构文件、轨迹文件（如 DCD、XTC）、拓扑文件等；具体格式取决于封装的工具。
- **演示与调试**：官方提供 Jupyter Notebook 演示工作流（在 GitHub 的 biobb_wf 仓库），可逐步执行并断点调试。
- **文档**：ReadTheDocs 提供详细 API 文档和示例。
- **GPU 需求**：取决于封装的工具（如 AMBER 的 PMEMD 支持 GPU），BioBB 本身不强制要求 GPU。

## 核心 idea
BioBB 的核心方法学是“标准化封装 + 工作流编排”：通过统一的 Python 接口和命令行约定，将异构的生物分子模拟工具抽象为可组合的“积木”，从而将复杂的多步骤模拟流程（如结构准备→MD→分析）转化为可复现、可共享的模块化流水线。其价值在于降低工具集成门槛，提升工作流的可移植性和可扩展性。

## 可搬移点
- **模块化封装模式**：可借鉴其“每个工具一个模块”的设计，将 AI 模型（如结构预测、构象生成）封装为类似 building block，便于集成到现有工作流。
- **标准输入/输出约定**：其统一的文件格式和参数规范可迁移至自定义 Pipeline，实现与现有生物信息学工具的无缝对接。
- **工作流适配器**：其 CWL/Galaxy/PyCOMPSs 适配器可复用，用于将 AI 模型部署到分布式计算环境。
- **License**：Apache 2.0，允许自由使用和修改，但需确认具体子模块的依赖许可。

Summary The [BioExcel Building Blocks](http://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb/) (BioBB) library is a collection of portable wrappers on top of common biomolecular simulation tools [Andrio, P., _et al_. BioExcel Building Blocks, a software library for interoperable biomolecular simulation workflows. _Sci Data_ **6**, 169 (2019)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-019-0177-4). Created and implemented within the [BioExcel CoE](http://bioexcel.eu/), the library is designed to i) increase the interoperability between the tools wrapped; ii) ease the implementation of biomolecular simulation workflows; and iii) increase the reusability and reproducibility of the generated workflows. The library is being developed following the FAIR principles for research software development best practices. The result is a collection of building block modules, classified according to the tool being wrapped (e.g. [biobb_amber](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_amber) for AMBER MD package) or the functionalities offered by the tools being wrapped (e.g. [biobb_vs](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_vs) for Virtual Screening, [biobb_chemistry](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_chemistry) for chemoinformatics). Each of the module is built from a combination of software packaging ([Pip](https://pypi.org/search/?q=biobb), [BioConda](https://bioconda.github.io/search.html?q=biobb), [BioContainers](https://biocontainers.pro/registry?all_fields_search=biobb)), documentation ([ReadTheDocs](https://biobb.readthedocs.io/), [OpenAPI](https://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb-api/rest), [Swagger](https://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb-api/rest/swagger.json)), registry and findability ([bio.tools](https://bio.tools/biobb), [BioSchemas](https://bioschemas.org/profiles/ComputationalTool/0.5-DRAFT/), [OpenEBench](https://openebench.bsc.es/tool/biobb), [WorkflowHub](https://workflowhub.eu/programmes/2)), source code ([GitHub](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb)) and WfMS integration -adapters- ([CWL](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_adapters/tree/master/biobb_adapters/cwl), [Galaxy](https://toolshed.g2.bx.psu.edu/repository?repository_id=e23296b413014cfc), [PyCOMPSs](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_adapters/tree/master/biobb_adapters/pycompss), [Jupyter Notebook](http://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb/workflows)).  A collection of [demonstration workflows](http://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb/workflows) have been developed to showcase the library possibilities. Built using the Jupyter Noteboook GUI, the demonstration workflows offer a graphical and interactive interface, including documentation (integrated markdown) related to the workflow and the building blocks used, and also information about the pipeline and the biomolecular simulation methods used. The set of demonstration workflows are available separately on the [BioExcel GitHub](https://github.com/orgs/bioexcel/repositories?q=biobb_wf&type=all&language=&sort=) repository, with step-by-step instructions on how to reproduce them in a local machine using the Conda packaging software. There is also a [global repository for all the BioExcel Building Blocks Workflows](https://github.com/bioexcel/biobb_workflows). In this repository, there are all the versions for each workflow manager: Common Workflow Language (CWL), Galaxy, Jupyter Notebooks and Pure Python. All the information regarding the BioExcel Building Blocks library can be found in the central [BioBB web page](http://mmb.irbbarcelona.org/biobb/). Links to source code, documentation, packages, containers, tutorials, and information from training events (e.g. BioExcel Summer/Winter School) can be found in the different web sections. ## 是什么

FoldMatch 是一个 Python 工具包，用于将大分子 3D 结构编码为固定长度的向量嵌入，以支持大规模的结构相似性搜索和聚类。它利用 ESM3 蛋白质语言模型计算残基级嵌入，并通过基于 Transformer 的聚合器网络生成结构级嵌入，最终通过 FAISS 实现快速相似性检索。

## 亮点

- **多级嵌入**：支持从 3D 结构（mmCIF/PDB）和 FASTA 序列（无需结构）计算残基级和结构级嵌入，灵活性高。
- **两阶段序列搜索**：嵌入预过滤后，使用原生 SIMD 内核进行精确的 Smith-Waterman 比对，报告序列同一性、覆盖率和校准的 E-value，兼顾速度与准确性。
- **高性能索引**：基于 FAISS 支持 flat、HNSW、IVF-PQ 等多种索引类型，并针对大规模数据库（如 3000 万条序列）进行了优化，提供多线程和 GPU 加速选项。
- **可扩展聚类**：提供 Leiden 和贪心两种聚类方法，其中贪心方法支持流式处理，适用于内存无法容纳完整相似性图的超大规模数据集。
- **工程化完善**：提供 CLI 和 Python API，支持分布式多节点/多 GPU 推理，并包含详尽的测试套件。

## 为何对本课题有用

FoldMatch 直接服务于蛋白质结构相似性搜索和聚类，是蛋白质结构 × AI 计算模拟课题中的关键工具。其核心价值在于：

- **结构比较加速**：将结构比对（如 TM-score）转化为嵌入空间的余弦距离，极大加速大规模结构数据库的搜索，可用于蛋白质结构分类、功能注释和进化分析。
- **序列-结构关联**：通过序列嵌入和结构嵌入的统一，支持从序列直接预测结构相似性，为结构预测结果的后处理提供快速评估手段。
- **可迁移的嵌入聚合方法**：其 Transformer 聚合器网络的设计思路可迁移至其他蛋白质结构表示学习任务，如构象采样中的状态表示或分子对接中的结合位点表征。
- **两阶段搜索范式**：嵌入预过滤 + 精确比对的两阶段策略，可借鉴到蛋白质-蛋白质相互作用预测或药物筛选中的候选物筛选流程。

## 怎么用

- **安装**：`pip install foldmatch`（Python ≥ 3.12），或从源码安装（需 C 编译器编译原生 Smith-Waterman 内核）。
- **CLI 使用**：
  - 计算嵌入：`fm-embedding from-structures residue --src-folder data/pdb --output-folder out/residue --structure-format mmcif`
  - 构建数据库：`fm-search build structures --structure-folder data/pdb --output-db dbs/my_db --tmp-embedding-folder tmp`
  - 查询：`fm-search query structure --db-path dbs/my_db --query-structure q.cif --output-file hits.tsv`
  - 聚类：`fm-search cluster --db-path dbs/my_db --output-file clusters.tsv`
- **Python API**：
  ```python
  from foldmatch import FoldMatch
  model = FoldMatch(min_res=10, max_res=5000)
  emb = model.structure_embedding("1abc.cif", structure_format="mmcif", chain_id="A")
  ```
- **输入/输出**：输入支持 mmCIF、PDB、FASTA；输出为 TSV 格式，包含查询 ID、目标 ID、嵌入相似度分数及可选的序列比对统计。
- **GPU 加速**：推荐使用 CUDA 支持以加速嵌入计算和 FAISS 索引构建。
- **测试**：运行 `pytest` 执行测试套件，可参考 `examples/` 目录中的示例。

## 核心 idea

FoldMatch 的核心方法学在于**将结构相似性学习转化为嵌入空间中的余弦距离回归问题**。它通过 ESM3 提取残基级特征，再用 Transformer 聚合器将可变长度的残基嵌入压缩为固定长度的结构级向量，训练目标直接逼近 TM-score。这种端到端的表示学习使得结构比较从昂贵的 3D 对齐转变为快速的向量运算，同时保持了生物学意义上的相似性度量。

## 可搬移点

- **Transformer 聚合器网络**（`src/foldmatch/model/residue_embedding_aggregator.py`）：可解耦并重新训练，用于其他蛋白质结构表示任务，如构象编码或结合位点嵌入。
- **两阶段搜索流程**（`src/foldmatch/search/`）：嵌入预过滤 + Smith-Waterman 精确比对的模式可移植到任何需要快速近似搜索后精确验证的场景。
- **原生 SIMD Smith-Waterman 内核**（`src/foldmatch/_native/fmsw/`）：可独立编译使用，加速序列比对。
- **FAISS 索引构建与查询封装**（`src/foldmatch/search/faiss_database.py`）：可复用为通用向量检索模块。
- **License**：Cambrian Non-Commercial License，非商业用途可自由使用，商业用途需确认。
readme:
# FoldMatch

**Version** 0.12.0


## Overview

FoldMatch is a Python toolkit to encode macromolecular 3D structures into fixed-length vector embeddings for efficient large-scale structure similarity search and clustering.

Reference: [Multi-scale structural similarity embedding search across entire proteomes](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag058).

A web-based implementation using this tool for structure similarity search is available at [RCSB.org](https://www.rcsb.org/search/advanced) under **3D Similarity**.

If you are interested in training a new model with a new structure dataset, visit the [rcsb-embedding-search repository](https://github.com/bioinsilico/rcsb-embedding-search), which provides scripts and documentation for training.


## Features

- **Residue-level embeddings** computed using the ESM3 protein language model
- **Sequence-based embeddings** from FASTA files without requiring 3D structures
- **Structure-level embeddings** aggregated via a transformer-based aggregator network 
- **Fast and efficient** FAISS-based similarity search
- **Two-stage sequence search** — an embedding prefilter followed by exact pairwise Smith-Waterman alignment on FoldMatch's native SIMD kernel, reporting sequence identity, coverage, and calibrated E-values over selectable output columns
- **Structural clustering**: Leiden (python-igraph) on the similarity graph, or greedy representatives in one streamed pass for collections whose graph does not fit in memory
- **Command-line interface** implemented with Typer for high-throughput inference workflows  
- **Python API** for interactive embedding computation and integration into analysis pipelines  
- **High-performance inference** leveraging PyTorch Lightning, with multi-node and multi-GPU support  

---

## Installation

### From PyPI

```bash
pip install foldmatch
```

### From Source (Development)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rcsb/foldmatch.git
cd foldmatch
pip install -e .
```

**Requirements:**

- Python ≥ 3.12
- ESM 3.2.3
- Lightning 2.6.1
- Typer 0.24.1
- Biotite 1.7.1
- FAISS 1.15.1 (the `faiss-cpu` wheel)
- igraph 1.0.0
- PyTorch with CUDA support (recommended for GPU acceleration)
- A C compiler (GCC 12 or later, or Clang 14 or later) when FoldMatch is built from source (an install from the
  sdist, `pip install -e .`): it compiles the native Smith-Waterman kernel of the sequence search's Stage 2. The
  platform wheels (Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS arm64 and x86_64) include it. Without a compiler the install
  still succeeds, with a warning, as a pure-Python package in which Stage 2 refuses to run and prints the reinstall
  command; everything else works.

**Optional Dependencies:**

- `faiss-gpu` for GPU-accelerated similarity search (instead of `faiss-cpu`)
- a FAISS built on MKL, for faster `ivf_pq` builds of large databases on Linux x86_64 with Python 3.12 (see *FAISS
  threads* below)

### FAISS threads

FoldMatch installs the `faiss-cpu` 1.15.1 wheel. On Linux the wheel bundles an OpenMP build of OpenBLAS
(`faiss_cpu.libs/libopenblaso-*.so`) and its own `libgomp`. FAISS's BLAS work therefore runs on FAISS's OpenMP
threads: the k-means and OPQ steps of an `ivf_pq` training, the IVF assignment of its adds, and batched flat searches.
Earlier FoldMatch versions pinned `faiss-cpu` 1.13.2, whose OpenBLAS is single-threaded. With it, a 30-million-entry
`ivf_pq` index took about 7 hours on any node.

- **Choosing the threads.** Export `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to set FAISS's threads. It also sets the threads of FAISS's
  OpenBLAS. `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` has no effect on FAISS's OpenBLAS; it changes only the OpenBLAS copies of numpy
  and scipy. When `OMP_NUM_THREADS` is unset, `fm-search build sequences-index` gives FAISS the physical cores it may
  use and logs the count.
- **Build times.** On NERSC Perlmutter, `fm-search build sequences-index --residue-codes` over 30.4 million sequences
  built the `ivf_pq` index in 1 h 45 min on a GPU node (one 64-core AMD EPYC 7763, 64 threads; 2 h 47 min for the
  whole command) and in 2 h 37 min on a CPU node (two 64-core EPYC 7763, 128 threads; 3 h 33 min). Most of the
  difference is the training, 40 min against 1 h 16 min: the OPQ step of the wheel's training does not gain from
  more threads. In a benchmark on the CPU node, two OPQ iterations took 66 to 70 s at 4 to 16 threads and 173 s at
  128, while 10 iterations of the IVF k-means gained up to about 32 threads.
- **Recommended on large nodes.** With the wheel, run `build sequences-index` with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=64` on a node
  with more than 64 physical cores, such as a 128-core CPU node. The setting applies to the whole command. This
  advice rests on the 64-thread GPU-node build above and on the OPQ benchmark (121 s at 64 threads against 173 s at
  128); a full build at 64 threads on a 128-core node was not timed. With it, `build sequences-index` warns that FAISS
  has fewer threads than physical cores; with the wheel that warning is expected. With the MKL build below, leave
  `OMP_NUM_THREADS` unset: it built a 30-million-entry index in 43 minutes at 128 threads.
- **128 BLAS threads at most.** The x86_64 wheel's OpenBLAS is built with `MAX_THREADS=128`, so FAISS's BLAS work
  runs on at most 128 threads. That OpenBLAS also lowers a higher OpenMP thread count to 128 when FAISS calls it. On
  a node with more than 128 physical cores, FAISS therefore runs 128 threads, and `build sequences-index` warns that
  FAISS has fewer threads than physical cores.
- **Reproducibility.** Two `hnsw` or `ivf_pq` builds are byte-identical only at `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`. The wheel's
  k-means results also change with the thread count. `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` alone does not make FAISS
  single-threaded. With the wheel, search results can change with FAISS's thread count too, in the last digits of
  the scores and so in the order of tied hits: between 32 and 256 threads, about a quarter of 1,000 batched flat
  searches and 3 to 5 `ivf_pq` searches were reordered. For bit-identical reruns, set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the same
  value (unset, FAISS gets each node's core count).
- **Existing databases.** FAISS 1.13.2 and 1.15.1 read each other's index files. Searching one database with either
  version gives the same hits up to float rounding (flat and `ivf_pq` scores within about 3e-7), which can reorder
  tied hits and swap hits tied at the cut-off; with `hnsw`, 5 to 7% of 1,000 searches changed at least one hit. A
  rebuilt `ivf_pq` index is a different, equally valid index: at 30 million entries, rebuilds shared 57 to 59% of
  their top-100 hits with each other (1.13.2 against the MKL build below, the wheel against the MKL build, and two
  wheel builds at 64 and 128 threads), with about the same self-hit rates. Searches whose results you compare should
  all use the same database.
- **Start-up log.** On Linux x86_64, `import faiss` logs at INFO `Could not load library with AVX2 support due to:
  ModuleNotFoundError("No module named 'faiss.swigfaiss_avx2'")`, then `Successfully loaded faiss.`. This is
  expected: the 1.15.1 wheel has one library, which picks the CPU's instructions at run time (its compile options
  include `DD`).
- **macOS.** The macOS wheel uses Apple Accelerate for BLAS and bundles its own `libomp`, so FoldMatch keeps
  `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` there by default (see *macOS notes*).

**Optional: FAISS with MKL.** For Linux x86_64 and Python 3.12 only, the official FAISS conda channel, `pytorch`,
publishes a `faiss-cpu` 1.15.1 build on MKL. It builds large `ivf_pq` indexes faster than the wheel, mostly because
its OPQ training is faster. On one NERSC Perlmutter GPU node (64 cores), `build sequences-index --residue-codes` over
30.4 million sequences took 2 h 02 min with it, of which 59 min was the index (the wheel: 2 h 47 min and 1 h 45 min).
In a FAISS-only script on one CPU node (2× AMD EPYC 7763), with 128 threads bound to cores (`OMP_PROC_BIND=spread
OMP_PLACES=cores`; FoldMatch does not bind threads), it built a 30-million-entry `ivf_pq` index in 43 minutes. The
commands below replace the wheel with the conda build. They were tested on NERSC, in a conda env (Python 3.12) in
which FoldMatch and its dependencies had been installed with `pip`:

```bash
python -m pip uninstall -y faiss-cpu
conda install -y --no-deps --override-channels -c pytorch -c conda-forge \
  "pytorch::faiss-cpu=1.15.1=py3.12_hf65b397_0_cpu" "pytorch::libfaiss=1.15.1=py3.12_hf65b397_0_cpu" \
  "conda-forge::mkl=2025.3.1=h0e700b2_12" "conda-forge::onemkl-license=2025.3.1=hf2ce2f3_12" \
  "conda-forge::tbb=2023.1.0=haa8c3ee_2" "conda-forge::libhwloc=2.15.0=default_hd7c4d0c_1001" \
  "conda-forge::libxml2=2.15.4=h7df9aa5_1" "conda-forge::libxml2-16=2.15.4=hf3af7cc_1" \
  "conda-forge::libiconv=1.18=h0cb94f2_3" "conda-forge::llvm-openmp=23.1.4=h7148c6a_0" \
  "conda-forge::_openmp_mutex=4.5=8_kmp_llvm" "conda-forge::libsvs-runtime=0.4.0=g7f7c639_0_0" \
  "conda-forge::python_abi=3.12=9_cp312" "conda-forge::libgcc=16.2.0=ha9f2e26_7" \
  "conda-forge::libgcc-ng=16.2.0=h69a702a_7" "conda-forge::libgomp=16.2.0=he0feb66_7" \
  "conda-forge::libstdcxx=16.2.0=h934c35e_7"
python -c "import faiss; print(faiss.__version__, faiss.get_compile_options())"   # 1.15.1 OPTIMIZE AVX2 ...
```

- **Why `--no-deps`.** It keeps conda from replacing pip's numpy and its BLAS, but conda then checks nothing. The
  listed packages are what `libfaiss` and MKL needed in that env, which had the rest; `libfaiss` needs `libgcc` 16 or
  later. In another env, a library still missing makes `import faiss` fail with an `ImportError` that names it.
- **Reinstalling FoldMatch.** The conda package registers as the distribution `faiss`, not `faiss-cpu`, so `pip check`
  reports `foldmatch ... requires faiss-cpu, which is not installed`. That is expected. Reinstall or upgrade FoldMatch
  in this env only with `pip install --no-deps ...`. Without `--no-deps`, pip installs the `faiss-cpu` wheel over the
  conda FAISS.
- **Updating the env.** Never run `conda update`, or a `conda install` without `--no-deps`, in this env: conda's view
  of it is inconsistent on purpose. Repeat the `--no-deps` form instead.
- **OpenMP runtime.** It depends on the import order. FoldMatch's commands load torch first, so torch's `libgomp`
  serves FAISS and MKL. A script that imports `faiss` first gets LLVM's `libomp`. Both work.
- **Thread logs.** threadpoolctl 3.6.0 does not list this MKL, so the index phase's `Thread pool:` lines do not show
  FAISS's BLAS.



## Usage

The package provides two main interfaces:
1. **Command-line Interface (CLI)** for batch processing and high-throughput workflows
2. **Python API** for interactive use and integration into custom pipelines

---

## Command-Line Interface (CLI)

The toolkit ships two CLIs, `fm-embedding` and `fm-search`. Each is invoked with `--help` for full option documentation; the canonical examples below are enough to get started.

### `fm-embedding` — compute embeddings

Two subcommand groups reflect input modality:

```bash
# Output folders must exist; give each kind of embedding its own (residue and chain files share names)
mkdir -p out/residue out/chain out/assembly out/seq-residue out/seq-chain

# Residue / chain / assembly embeddings from a folder of 3D structures
fm-embedding from-structures residue  --src-folder data/pdb --output-folder out/residue  --structure-format mmcif
fm-embedding from-structures chain    --src-folder data/pdb --output-folder out/chain    --structure-format mmcif
fm-embedding from-structures assembly --src-folder data/pdb --output-folder out/assembly --structure-format mmcif

# Residue / chain embeddings from protein sequences in a FASTA file (no 3D required)
fm-embedding from-sequences  residue  --fasta-file seqs.fasta --output-folder out/seq-residue
fm-embedding from-sequences  chain    --fasta-file seqs.fasta --output-folder out/seq-chain

# One-shot model download
fm-embedding download-models
```

Assembly-level embeddings are only available under `from-structures` — there is no assembly concept for a bare sequence.

Each FASTA record's embedding is stored under its id, the first word of its header, so `from-sequences` refuses a repeated id before ESM3 is loaded. With `--output-format csv` or `pt` (one file per record or chain), an id is a file name: one that holds `/` or cannot name a file, ids that the output folder takes for one file (`abc` and `ABC` on macOS's default file system), and a `--fasta-file` named like an output are refused too, and a run stops at a second write of one file (chains `A` and `a` of one structure on macOS). Parquet and JSON keep any id. A rerun into the same folder replaces its own files, as before.

`from-sequences residue` and `from-sequences chain` take `--output-codes-folder FOLDER`: the same ESM3 pass also computes each sequence's residue codes, the 8-byte per-residue ESM3 codes that `fm-search build sequences --residue-codes` stores (esm-codes-v1 target codes: 8 integers, 0-255, per residue), and writes them to that folder. ESM3 runs once; the embedding files are byte for byte those of a run without the option, and the output folder holds them only, so `fm-search build embeddings` and `query embedding` read it as before (for chain embeddings). The codes folder must exist and must not be `--output-folder` (compared as folders on disk: a symbolic link, `.`, or another case of the name on macOS are the same folder; a usage error, exit status 2); a subfolder of it, or a folder that holds it, will do (`fm-search` reads the files of a folder, not its subfolders), unless it is named as a file of the other folder's output. The codes follow `--output-format`, in the layout of the embeddings, one `[L, 8]` table per sequence of `L` residues, one row per residue: row `i` of the codes is residue `i`, which is row `i + 1` of the residue embeddings (`[L + 2, 1536]`, ESM3's BOS and EOS rows included):

| Format | Residue-code files in the codes folder | Layout |
|---|---|---|
| `csv` | `<id>.csv`, as the embedding is `<output-folder>/<id>.csv` | L lines of 8 integers, no header or index |
| `pt` | `<id>.pt` | a CPU `uint8` tensor `[L, 8]` |
| `parquet` | `<output-codes-name>-<rank>.parquet` | columns `id`, `residue_codes` (`list<fixed_size_list<uint8, 8>>`), `seq_sha1`; the schema metadata names the scoring system, its digests and the pass (`--min-res-n`, device, ranks, versions) |
| `json` | `<output-codes-name>-<rank>.json.gz` | records `{"id", "residue_codes"}`, a list of 8 integers per residue |

`--output-codes-name NAME` names the parquet and json files (default `<output-name>-codes`; the output name itself is allowed, as the folders differ); like `--output-name`, it names no csv or pt file. It is refused without `--output-codes-folder`. Before ESM3 is loaded, a run with `--output-codes-folder` refuses a codes name that cannot name those files, ids (csv, pt) that the codes folder takes for one file, a `--fasta-file` named like a code file, one folder inside the other under the name of a file that the other one gets (`out/<id>.csv` as the codes folder of a csv run, say), and FASTA records whose sequence holds `<`, `>` or non-ASCII characters (as the build does). Nor does any `fm-embedding` run replace a file of the other kind: before ESM3 (exit status 1), it refuses to replace an embedding file in its codes folder (an earlier run's output folder given as the codes folder, say) or a residue-code file in its output folder, with or without `--output-codes-folder`; files of other names are left alone, and a rerun into the same folders replaces its own files as before. The esm-codes bundle (~26 MB) is downloaded once, as for builds; on several nodes, or ranks started by `srun` or `torchrun`, run `fm-embedding download-models` first. A sequence whose codes cannot be computed (ESM3's rows do not match its length) is logged as an ERROR and gets an empty table (an empty file in csv); the run still writes every file, then exits with status 1, naming how many sequences got no codes, the first ids and where their empty tables are. With several devices or nodes, each rank that ends its pass waits for the others, and rank 0 then fails for the whole run (the other ranks log their count), so that no rank fails while another one still writes: the exit status is 1 under Lightning's own launcher, `srun` or `torchrun` alike. The code files are neither embeddings nor embedding shards: `fm-search build embeddings`, `query embedding` and `build residue-codes --from-shards` refuse them if they are moved among embedding files.

```bash
mkdir -p out/seq-chain out/seq-codes
fm-embedding from-sequences chain --fasta-file seqs.fasta --output-folder out/seq-chain \
    --output-format parquet --output-codes-folder out/seq-codes
# out/seq-chain/inference-0.parquet (chain embeddings), out/seq-codes/inference-codes-0.parquet (residue codes)
fm-search build embeddings --embedding-folder out/seq-chain --output-db db/chains
```

Run `fm-embedding [from-structures|from-sequences] [command] --help` for full options (batch size, accelerator, devices, output format, distributed settings, etc.).

### `fm-search` — build and query FAISS databases

```bash
# Build a similarity-search database from structures, FASTA, or pre-computed embeddings
fm-search build structures  --structure-folder data/pdb --output-db dbs/my_db --tmp-embedding-folder tmp
fm-search build sequences   --fasta-file seqs.fasta     --output-db dbs/my_db --tmp-embedding-folder tmp
fm-search build embeddings  --embedding-folder out/chain --output-db dbs/my_db

# Query the database (--output-file is required)
fm-search query structure   --db-path dbs/my_db --query-structure q.cif --output-file hits.tsv
fm-search query sequences   --db-path dbs/my_db --fasta-file q.fasta --tmp-embedding-folder tmp --output-file hits.tsv
fm-search query embedding   --db-path dbs/my_db --embedding-folder out/chain --output-file hits.tsv
fm-search query db          --query-db-path dbs/queries --subject-db-path dbs/my_db --output-file hits.tsv

# Inspect, cluster, export
fm-search stats             --db-path dbs/my_db
fm-search cluster           --db-path dbs/my_db --output-file clusters.tsv
fm-search cluster           --db-path dbs/my_db --output-file clusters.tsv --method greedy
fm-search similarity-graph  --db-path dbs/my_db --output-file graph.graphml
```

All `build` commands accept `--index-type [auto|flat|hnsw|ivf_pq]` and IVF-PQ tuning flags (`--ivf-nlist`, `--ivf-nprobe`). See `fm-search <subcommand> --help` for the full surface.

`cluster` and `similarity-graph` work on every database type. On `ivf_pq` a score is estimated from the PQ codes (the chain's decoded embedding, normalised, against each stored code, as in `query db`), so two identical chains score close to, but not exactly, 1. With `--method leiden` (the default) the k-NN search takes time in proportion to the number of chains and `--max-neighbors`, whatever `--threshold`; `--method greedy` searches only chains no representative has taken, so its time also depends on `--threshold` and on database order. The graph's memory grows with the number of edges, which `--threshold` and `--max-neighbors` bound (at most `--max-neighbors` edges from each chain's search), and the Leiden step's memory also grows with the number of chains. The Leiden step of `cluster` runs on one CPU thread. It runs a fixed number of iterations of python-igraph's Leiden (modularity at `--resolution`), 10 unless `--leiden-iterations` says otherwise; `--seed` makes it repeatable.

`cluster --method greedy` clusters collections whose similarity graph does not fit in memory. When most chains have `--max-neighbors` neighbours above `--threshold`, the Leiden route keeps about `n x --max-neighbors / 2` edges for `n` chains: 447,547,205 edges for 1,000,000 chains in an `ivf_pq` database (`--max-neighbors 1000`, `--threshold 0.8`), about 15.1e9 for 30.4M chains (`ivf_pq`); with fewer neighbours above the threshold, fewer (219,292,519 for the same 1,000,000 chains on `hnsw`, where few chains reach `--max-neighbors`). Leiden's memory grows with the edges (on that 1M-chain `ivf_pq` database, `cluster` peaked at 28.16 GiB, about 66 bytes an edge above the memory before the load, on Linux x86_64 at 128 threads), greedy's with the chains: it picks representatives in one streamed pass over the database, dropping each block's search results once used. A cluster is a representative and the still-unclustered chains among its `--max-neighbors` nearest that score at least `--threshold` (MMseqs2/CD-HIT style): chains are taken in database order, and a chain in no cluster yet becomes a representative. When most representatives have `--max-neighbors` neighbours above the threshold (the statistics report the share; 98.96% of rows in the first 10 blocks of a 30.4M-chain `ivf_pq` database), clusters are bounded by `--max-neighbors`, and a representative or singleton can score above the threshold with an earlier representative. Greedy clusters are smaller and tighter than Leiden's few large communities at 0.8: higher family purity, lower completeness and family ARI (measured at 100k and 1M chains). Results depend on database order (the order chains were added), as CD-HIT's depend on length order. `--max-neighbors` caps cluster size at `--max-neighbors` + 1 chains (on `hnsw`, FAISS's `efSearch` of 16 returns fewer: 481.7 of 1000 on average on a 100k-chain database, so a larger value adds few). Greedy needs no graph and computes no modularity; it has no resolution or iteration count and is deterministic, so `--resolution`, `--leiden-iterations` and `--seed` are refused with it.

#### Output format

Every command writes **tab-separated rows** to `--output-file` — one record per line. `query` results are ordered best-first per query, so rank is simply the row order.

`--output-file` cannot be one of the command's inputs: a file of a database it reads (`<db path>.index`, `.metadata`, `.invlists`, `.sequences` or `.rescodes.*`), the query FASTA or structure file, or a query embedding file; such a run is refused before any work. A file written by an earlier command is replaced. `query embedding` refuses query embeddings that share an id (results are kept by query id).

`--format-mode` selects the file layout:

| Mode | Layout |
|---|---|
| `headless_tsv` *(default)* | Tab-separated, **no header row** |
| `tsv` | Tab-separated, with a header row naming each column |

```bash
# Add a header row naming the columns
fm-search query sequences --db-path dbs/my_db --fasta-file q.fasta \
    --tmp-embedding-folder tmp --output-file hits.tsv --format-mode tsv
```

The header always names the columns actually emitted, in the order emitted — for a
sequence-identity search that is your `--format-output` selection. `--format-mode`
controls only the file's shape; `--format-output` controls which columns it holds.

An **embedding-only** search — `query structure`, `query embedding`, or any query whose database has no sequence store — emits three columns:

```
query   target   embscore
```

A **sequence-identity** search (Stage 2, below) emits the columns chosen with `--format-output`, which default to those same three followed by the alignment statistics.

`cluster` uses the same convention with its own columns:

```
chain_id   cluster_id   cluster_size
```

and, with `--method greedy`, a fourth column, the representative's chain id (equal to `chain_id` on the representative's own row):

```
chain_id   cluster_id   cluster_size   representative
```

`cluster_id` 0 is the largest cluster, under both methods (ties under greedy in representative order). Rows are in database order; `--min-cluster-size` drops the rows of smaller clusters.

(`similarity-graph` is the one exception: GraphML is a graph format, not tabular.)

#### Two-stage sequence search (exact identity)

`build sequences` also writes a sidecar `{db}.sequences` store next to the FAISS index. This lets sequence-built databases report **exact** sequence identity, not just embedding similarity: when you run `query sequences` (or `query db`) against such a database, a second stage pairwise-aligns each embedding hit (local Smith-Waterman, BLOSUM62) and re-ranks the surviving hits by bitscore.

Stage 2 aligns on FoldMatch's native SIMD Smith-Waterman kernel, a compiled library (see *Requirements*). It reproduces biotite 1.7.1's `align_optimal` (local, affine gaps), ties included, which Stage 2 used before: the same scores, coordinates and alignments, so the same output. Without the kernel, `query sequences` and `query db` refuse to run Stage 2 before the queries are embedded or the database is searched, and print the command that rebuilds it; `--no-seq-identity` still runs an embedding-only search.

Stage-2 hits use the same **tab-separated, no-header** format as every other query output. Pick the columns with `--format-output`:

```bash
# Stage 2 turns on automatically when the database has a sequence store
fm-search query sequences --db-path dbs/my_db --fasta-file q.fasta \
    --tmp-embedding-folder tmp --output-file hits.tsv

# Choose the output columns
fm-search query sequences --db-path dbs/my_db --fasta-file q.fasta \
    --tmp-embedding-folder tmp --output-file hits.tsv \
    --format-output "query,target,evalue,qaln,taln"
```

Default columns: `query,target,embscore,fident,alnlen,mismatch,gapopen,qstart,qend,tstart,tend,evalue,bits`.

Supported `--format-output` fields:

| Field | Meaning | Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|-------|---------|
| `query` | Query sequence identifier | `tlen` | Target sequence length |
| `target` | Target sequence identifier | `alnlen` | Alignment length (aligned columns) |
| `embscore` | Stage-1 embedding similarity score | `raw` | Raw alignment score |
| `evalue` | E-value | `bits` | Bit score (integer) |
| `gapopen` | Number of gap **open events** (not gap chars) | `cigar` | CIGAR string (`M` match, `D` gap in query, `I` gap in target) |
| `pident` | Percentage of identical matches | `qseq` / `tseq` | Query / target sequence |
| `fident` | Fraction of identical matches | `qaln` / `taln` | Aligned query / target sequence with gaps |
| `nident` | Number of identical matches | `mismatch` | Number of mismatches |
| `qstart` / `qend` | 1-indexed alignment bounds in query | `qcov` / `tcov` | Fraction of query / target covered |
| `qlen` | Query sequence length | | |
| `tstart` / `tend` | 1-indexed alignment bounds in target | | |

- **Auto by default**: Stage 2 runs when the database(s) carry a sequence store and falls back to embedding-only otherwise. Force it with `--seq-identity` (errors if no store is present) or disable with `--no-seq-identity`. `query db` requires **both** databases to have sequence stores.
- Hits below `--min-seq-identity` (default `0.3`) or `--min-coverage` (default `0.8`) are dropped, as are hits above `--max-evalue` (default `1e-3`; pass `inf` to keep every hit). `--max-evalue` turns the significance pass on even when neither `evalue` nor `bits` is in `--format-output`.
- Tuning: `--gap-open` (default `11`) and `--gap-extend` (default `1`), where a gap of length L costs gap-open + (L − 1) × gap-extend, and `--align-workers` (defaults to all CPUs on the node). `--gap-open` must be at least 1 and `--gap-extend` at least 0, both at most 1,048,576; the sign is ignored. With `--significance-mode default`, a run that needs significance (an `evalue` or `bits` column, or a finite `--max-evalue`, which the default `1e-3` is) needs the gap costs 11/1: for other gap costs use `--significance-mode sampled`, or `--max-evalue inf` with neither column in `--format-output`. Both rules are checked before the queries are embedded (`query sequences`) or the database is searched (`query db`).
- Compositional bias correction: off by default, so alignments are scored with plain BLOSUM62. `--comp-bias-corr` (scaled by `--comp-bias-corr-scale`, default `1`) applies mmseqs's correction for locally biased amino-acid composition, which mmseqs enables by default; use it when comparing with `mmseqs search`. With the same setting on both tools, raw scores, bit scores and E-values match `mmseqs search` (18-8cc5c) on the same pairs, except for alignments containing a non-standard residue (`X`, `B`, `Z`, `J`, `U`, `O`, `*`), which the two tools score differently. The correction can shorten alignments over biased regions, so coordinates, identity and coverage change too.
- `evalue`/`bits` use calibrated Karlin–Altschul statistics by default (`--significance-mode default`). `--significance-mode sampled` estimates λ/K by sampling for other gap penalties, but its absolute magnitudes are relative-only. The significance pass is skipped automatically when neither `evalue` nor `bits` is in `--format-output`.

---

## Python API

The `FoldMatch` class provides methods for computing embeddings programmatically.

### Basic Usage

```python
from foldmatch import FoldMatch

# Initialize model
model = FoldMatch(min_res=10, max_res=5000)

# Load models (optional - loads automatically on first use)
model.load_models()  # Auto-detects CUDA
# or specify device:
# import torch
# model.load_models(device=torch.device("cuda:0"))
```

A protein chain is embedded only if it has at least `min_res` residues (default 10), counted as polymer amino-acid residues: free amino acids are not counted. With `max_res` (default `None`, no limit), a structure method raises `ValueError`, before any ESM3 pass, when the protein chains it is about to embed have more than `max_res` residues together, counted the same way: the chains with `chain_id` (in an assembly, one per copy), else every protein chain of the structure or assembly. `sequence_embedding` raises `ValueError` when the sequence is shorter than `min_res` or longer than `max_res`.

### Methods

#### `load_models(device=None)`

Load both residue and aggregator models.

```python
import torch
model.load_models(device=torch.device("cuda"))
```

---

#### `load_residue_embedding(device=None)`

Load only the ESM3 residue embedding model.

```python
model.load_residue_embedding()
```

---

#### `load_aggregator_embedding(device=None)`

Load only the aggregator model.

```python
model.load_aggregator_embedding()
```

---

#### `residue_embedding(src_structure, structure_format='mmcif', chain_id=None, assembly_id=None)`

Compute per-residue embeddings for a structure.

**Parameters:**
- `src_structure`: File path, URL, or file-like object
- `structure_format`: `'mmcif'`, `'binarycif'`, or `'pdb'`
- `chain_id`: Chain ID (optional): the protein chains with this ID (in an assembly, one per copy); every protein chain if None
- `assembly_id`: Assembly ID for biological assembly (optional)

**Returns:** `torch.Tensor` of shape `[L + 2, 1536]` for one chain of `L` residues: one row per residue, between ESM3's BOS and EOS rows. Several chains give their tensors one after another, each with its BOS and EOS rows. Raises `ValueError` when no protein chain qualifies, or when `max_res` is exceeded.

```python
# Single chain
residue_emb = model.residue_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    chain_id="A"
)

# All chains concatenated
all_residues = model.residue_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif"
)

# Biological assembly
assembly_residues = model.residue_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    assembly_id="1"
)
```

---

#### `residue_embedding_by_chain(src_structure, structure_format='mmcif', chain_id=None)`

Compute per-residue embeddings separately for each chain.

**Returns:** `dict[str, torch.Tensor]` mapping each chain ID to its embeddings, of shape `[L + 2, 1536]`; `{}` when no chain qualifies

```python
chain_embeddings = model.residue_embedding_by_chain(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif"
)
# Returns: {'A': tensor(...), 'B': tensor(...), ...}

# Get specific chain
chain_a = model.residue_embedding_by_chain(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    chain_id="A"
)
```

---

#### `residue_embedding_by_assembly(src_structure, structure_format='mmcif', assembly_id=None)`

Compute residue embeddings for an assembly.

**Returns:** `dict[str, torch.Tensor]` mapping the assembly ID (`'0'` for the asymmetric unit when `assembly_id` is None) to the tensors of its protein chains (one per copy) one after another, each with its BOS and EOS rows; `{}` when no chain qualifies

```python
assembly_emb = model.residue_embedding_by_assembly(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    assembly_id="1"
)
# Returns: {'1': tensor(...)}
```

---

#### `sequence_embedding(sequence)`

Compute residue embeddings from amino acid sequence (no structural information).

**Parameters:**
- `sequence`: Amino acid sequence string (plain or FASTA format)

**Returns:** `torch.Tensor` of shape `[L + 2, 1536]` for a sequence of `L` residues (ESM3's BOS and EOS rows included)

```python
# Plain sequence
seq_emb = model.sequence_embedding("ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY")

# FASTA format
fasta = """>Protein1
ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY
ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY"""
seq_emb = model.sequence_embedding(fasta)
```

---

#### `aggregator_embedding(residue_embedding)`

Aggregate residue embeddings into a single structure-level vector.

**Parameters:**
- `residue_embedding`: `torch.Tensor` from any of the residue embedding methods (for `residue_embedding_by_chain` and `residue_embedding_by_assembly`, a value of their dict)

**Returns:** `torch.Tensor` of shape `[1536]`

```python
residue_emb = model.residue_embedding("1abc.cif", chain_id="A")
structure_emb = model.aggregator_embedding(residue_emb)
```

---

#### `structure_embedding(src_structure, structure_format='mmcif', chain_id=None, assembly_id=None)`

End-to-end: compute residue embeddings and aggregate in one call.

```python
# Complete structure embedding
structure_emb = model.structure_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    chain_id="A"
)
# Returns: tensor of shape [1536]
```

---

### Complete Example

```python
from foldmatch import FoldMatch
import torch

# Initialize
model = FoldMatch(min_res=10, max_res=5000)

# Option 1: Full structure embedding (one-shot)
embedding = model.structure_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    chain_id="A"
)

# Option 2: Step-by-step with residue embeddings
residue_emb = model.residue_embedding(
    src_structure="1abc.cif",
    structure_format="mmcif",
    chain_id="A"
)
structure_emb = model.aggregator_embedding(residue_emb)

# Option 3: Process multiple chains
chain_embeddings = model.residue_embedding_by_chain(
    src_structure="1abc.cif"
)
for chain_id, res_emb in chain_embeddings.items():
    chain_emb = model.aggregator_embedding(res_emb)
    print(f"Chain {chain_id}: {chain_emb.shape}")

# Sequence-based embedding
seq_emb = model.sequence_embedding("ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY")
structure_from_seq = model.aggregator_embedding(seq_emb)
```

See the `examples/` and `tests/` directories for more use cases.

---

## Model Architecture

The embedding model is trained to predict structural similarity by approximating TM-scores using cosine distances between embeddings. It consists of two main components:

- **Protein Language Model (PLM)**: Computes residue-level embeddings from a given 3D structure.
- **Residue Embedding Aggregator**: A transformer-based neural network that aggregates these residue-level embeddings into a single vector.

![Embedding model architecture](assets/embedding-model-architecture.png)

### **Protein Language Model (PLM)**
Residue-wise embeddings of protein structures are computed using the [ESM3](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/) generative protein language model.

### **Residue Embedding Aggregator**
The aggregation component consists of six transformer encoder layers, each with a 3,072-neuron feedforward layer and ReLU activations. After processing through these layers, a summation pooling operation is applied, followed by 12 fully connected residual layers that refine the embeddings into a single 1,536-dimensional vector.

---

## Testing

After installation, run the test suite:

```bash
pytest
```

### macOS notes

**The problem.** PyPI wheels for `faiss-cpu` and `torch` (pulled in via `lightning`) each bundle their own copy of `libomp.dylib`. On macOS, both copies get loaded into the same Python process. Whenever FAISS enters an OpenMP-parallel section (batched search with more than one query vector, `IndexHNSWFlat` graph construction, IVF-PQ training) the second OpenMP runtime fails to `pthread_mutex_init` and the call deadlocks — the CLI appears to hang indefinitely — or the process crashes (a segmentation fault at `OMP_NUM_THREADS=4` on an M1 Max, with torch 2.11 and `faiss-cpu` 1.13.2 or 1.15.1). Linux installs are unaffected: there the copies are GNU `libgomp` builds, which can be loaded together, and FoldMatch's commands, which load torch first, run FAISS on torch's copy.

**Affected commands** on macOS without mitigation:

- `fm-search build` with `--index-type hnsw` or `auto` past ~10k vectors, and any `--index-type ivf_pq`.
- `fm-search query embedding` with a multi-row `.parquet` file.
- `fm-search query sequences` with more than one input sequence.
- `fm-search query db` (database-to-database).
- `fm-search cluster` and `fm-search similarity-graph`, which search many chains per FAISS call (safe at the default `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` pin).

Single-query paths (`fm-search query structure`, small `--index-type flat` builds) are unaffected.

**Possible fixes.**

1. **Fix the install environment** — install both libraries against a unified OpenMP runtime. On conda-forge:
   ```bash
   conda install -c conda-forge faiss-cpu pytorch llvm-openmp
   ```
   Once a single libomp is loaded, FAISS's parallel paths just work and you keep the full multi-threaded performance.

2. **Force single-threaded FAISS via environment variable** — set `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` before invoking Python:
   ```bash
   export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
   fm-search query db ...
   ```
   Sidesteps the parallel section entirely. Toolkit works, but FAISS runs single-threaded so large builds and queries are slower.

**What this package does by default.** To prevent macOS users from hitting a silent hang out of the box, `foldmatch/__init__.py` calls `os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")` on `darwin` only — before any `torch` or `faiss` import. This is option 2 above, applied automatically. Linux installs are not touched (the branch is skipped). A user on macOS who has fixed their environment per option 1 can opt back into parallelism by exporting `OMP_NUM_THREADS=N` before launching Python — `setdefault` respects an existing value.

## 是什么

GPUMD-PySAGES 是一个 GPU 原生的接口层，用于将 GPUMD（一个高效的 GPU 分子动力学引擎）与 PySAGES（一个基于 JAX 的增强采样框架）连接起来。它使得在 GPUMD 的机器学习势（如 NEP 势）上运行增强采样分子动力学（如 metadynamics、ABF、伞形采样）成为可能，并实现了 GPU 到 GPU 的零拷贝数据交换。

## 亮点

- **零拷贝 GPU 数据交换**：通过 DLPack 协议，在 GPUMD 的 C++/CUDA 引擎和 PySAGES 的 JAX 计算图之间直接传递 GPU 数组，避免了主机与设备之间的数据传输，显著降低了接口开销。
- **原生 GPU 增强采样**：所有 collective variables 和 bias 计算均在 GPU 上通过 JAX 执行，无需 CPU 回退，充分利用了 GPU 算力。
- **自定义 CUDA 内核**：提供了一个专门的内核，将 JAX 计算出的 AOS 格式 bias 力直接加到 GPUMD 的 SOA 格式力缓冲区中，避免了格式转换开销。
- **模块化设计**：通过 `#ifdef USE_PYSAGES` 钩子，在 GPUMD 的 MD 循环中插入回调，保持了 GPUMD 核心代码的完整性，同时实现了功能扩展。
- **性能优化**：在 ethane 体系上，接口总开销仅为约 0.77 ms/步，其中快照重建占主导，但整体仍保持高效。

## 为何对本课题有用

该仓库直接面向蛋白质结构 × AI/计算模拟课题中的**增强采样分子动力学**需求。它允许在 GPUMD 的机器学习势（如 NEP）上运行 metadynamics 等增强采样方法，这对于蛋白质构象采样、自由能计算和构象生成至关重要。其零拷贝 DLPack 交换和 JAX 原生计算模式，为将 GPU 加速的 MD 引擎与基于 JAX 的 AI 模型（如 collective variable 的神经网络表示）集成提供了可复用的架构。此外，其自定义 CUDA 内核处理 AOS/SOA 格式转换的思路，可迁移到其他需要高效力场与 AI 模型交互的场景。

## 怎么用

- **主入口**：Python 接口 `gpumd.Simulation("run.in")` 加载 GPUMD 模拟，然后通过 `pysages.SamplingContext` 运行增强采样。
- **安装**：需要先编译 GPUMD（从源码），然后安装 PySAGES，最后通过 `build.sh` 或手动复制补丁文件并 `make pygpumd` 构建 Python 扩展。依赖包括 Python ≥ 3.8、pybind11、JAX with CUDA、CuPy、CUDA toolkit ≥ 11.0。
- **示例**：`examples/ethane-metad.py` 演示了乙烷二面角的 well-tempered metadynamics；`examples/diagnose_timing.py` 用于分析接口开销。
- **输入/输出**：输入为 GPUMD 的 `run.in` 文件（包含模拟参数），输出为 GPUMD 的轨迹和 PySAGES 的 bias 数据。
- **GPU 需求**：必须使用 NVIDIA GPU 和 CUDA 支持，因为整个流程依赖 GPU 加速。

## 核心 idea

核心方法学在于**通过 DLPack 实现跨语言、跨框架的 GPU 内存零拷贝共享**，并利用 JAX 的即时编译和自动微分能力，将增强采样中的 collective variable 计算和 bias 更新无缝嵌入到 MD 循环中，从而在不牺牲性能的前提下，将机器学习势与高级采样算法结合。

## 可搬移点

- **DLPack 交换模块**：`wrapper/gpumd_python.cpp` 中的 DLPack 封装逻辑，可解耦并用于其他需要将 C++/CUDA 引擎与 JAX/PyTorch 交互的场景，例如将蛋白质结构预测模型的输出直接用于 MD 模拟。
- **自定义 CUDA 内核**：`gpumd_python_kernels.cu` 中的 AOS-to-SOA bias 添加内核，可移植到其他需要高效力场与 AI 模型交互的 pipeline 中。
- **回调钩子机制**：`run.cuh`/`run.cu` 中的 `#ifdef USE_PYSAGES` 钩子设计，展示了如何在不修改核心引擎的情况下插入外部计算，可借鉴用于其他 MD 引擎的扩展。
- **License**：MIT License，允许自由使用和修改，但需确认与 GPUMD 的 GPL-3.0+ 兼容性（README 已说明兼容）。

# GPUMD-PySAGES
[![CI](https://github.com/JaafarMehrez/GPUMD-PySAGES/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/JaafarMehrez/GPUMD-PySAGES/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/1243030964.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20589485)

A GPU-native interface between [GPUMD](https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD) and [PySAGES](https://github.com/SSAGESLabs/PySAGES) for enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics on machine-learning potentials.

**Blog post:** [GPUMD-PySAGES: GPU-Native Enhanced Sampling on Machine-Learning Potentials](https://jaafarmehrez.github.io/blog/gpumd-pysages/)
— zero-copy DLPack exchange, JAX collective variables, and a well-tempered metadynamics example.

## Overview

This package bridges GPUMD (a highly efficient GPU MD engine) with PySAGES (a JAX-based enhanced-sampling framework). It enables:

- **Metadynamics**, **ABF**, **Umbrella Sampling**, and all PySAGES methods on GPUMD simulations.
- **Zero-copy GPU-to-GPU** data exchange via DLPack — no host-to-device transfers.
- **Native GPU execution** of collective-variable and bias computations via JAX.
- **NEP potentials** — run enhanced sampling on GPUMD's neural-network potentials with full GPU acceleration.

## Dependencies

- [GPUMD](https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD) (current master / v5.x — the interface targets the refactored codebase that uses `measure/` actions)
- [PySAGES](https://github.com/SSAGESLabs/PySAGES)
- Python ≥ 3.8
- pybind11
- JAX with CUDA support (`jax[cuda]`)
- CuPy
- CUDA toolkit ≥ 11.0

## Installation

### Step 1 — Install GPUMD

Clone and build GPUMD from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD.git
cd GPUMD/src
make gpumd
```

### Step 2 — Install PySAGES

```bash
git clone https://github.com/SSAGESLabs/PySAGES.git
cd PySAGES
pip install -e .
```

### Step 3 — Install this interface

```bash
git clone https://github.com/JaafarMehrez/GPUMD-PySAGES.git
cd GPUMD-PySAGES

# Option A: Build with the provided script (recommended)
./build.sh /path/to/GPUMD

# Option B: Manual — copy the modified GPUMD core files and build the wrapper
cd /path/to/GPUMD/src

# Backup the original files
cp main_gpumd/run.cuh       main_gpumd/run.cuh.bak
cp main_gpumd/run.cu        main_gpumd/run.cu.bak
cp utilities/gpu_vector.cuh utilities/gpu_vector.cuh.bak
cp makefile                 makefile.bak

# Copy the modified GPUMD core files (complete files, see gpumd_patches/)
cp /path/to/GPUMD-PySAGES/gpumd_patches/run.cuh        main_gpumd/
cp /path/to/GPUMD-PySAGES/gpumd_patches/run.cu         main_gpumd/
cp /path/to/GPUMD-PySAGES/gpumd_patches/gpu_vector.cuh utilities/
cp /path/to/GPUMD-PySAGES/gpumd_patches/makefile       .

# Copy the pybind11 wrapper files into the GPUMD source
cp /path/to/GPUMD-PySAGES/wrapper/* main_gpumd/

# Build the Python extension module
make pygpumd

# Install the PySAGES backend
pip install -e .
```

## Quick start

```python
import gpumd
import pysages
from pysages.colvars import Component
from pysages.methods import HarmonicBias

# Load GPUMD simulation (parses run.in)
sim = gpumd.Simulation("run.in")

# Define CV and sampling method
cv = Component([0], 2)  # z-coordinate of atom 0
method = HarmonicBias(cv, kspring=10.0, center=5.0)

# Run with PySAGES bias
with pysages.SamplingContext(method, lambda: sim) as ctx:
    ctx.run(1000)
```

See `examples/` for complete tutorials:
- `ethane-metad.py` — Well-tempered metadynamics of ethane H-C-C-H dihedral
- `diagnose_timing.py` — Profile the interface overhead

## Performance

Benchmarked on ethane (8 atoms, NEP4, 1M steps, RTX 3090):

| Stage | Time / step |
|-------|-------------|
| Snapshot (DLPack rebuild) | ~0.51 ms |
| JAX CV + bias compute | ~0.16 ms |
| Bias apply (custom CUDA kernel) | ~0.10 ms |
| **Total interface overhead** | **~0.77 ms** |


## Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PySAGES (JAX)                                              │
│  ├─ Collective Variables (Python / JAX)                     │
│  ├─ Bias computation (GPU, float64)                         │
│  └─ run() orchestration                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GPUMD-PySAGES Backend (pysages_backend/gpumd.py)           │
│  ├─ Snapshot from DLPack (zero-copy)                        │
│  ├─ Cached constants (ids, masses, box for NVT)             │
│  └─ _update() registered as GPUMD step callback             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  pybind11 Wrapper (wrapper/gpumd_python.cpp)                │
│  ├─ DLPack capsules for positions/forces/velocities         │
│  ├─ set_step_callback() / run()                             │
│  └─ add_aos_bias_to_forces() (custom CUDA kernel)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GPUMD Engine (C++ / CUDA)                                  │
│  ├─ force.compute()                                         │
│  ├─ step_callback()  ← PySAGES hook                         │
│  └─ integrate.compute2()                                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## How it works

1. **GPUMD core** (`run.cuh` / `run.cu`) — a minimal `#ifdef USE_PYSAGES` hook is added to the MD loop. It calls a Python callback after force computation and before integration.
2. **pybind11 wrapper** (`gpumd_python.cpp`) — exposes GPUMD's GPU arrays as DLPack capsules that JAX can read directly, and accepts bias forces from JAX to add back to GPUMD's force buffer.
3. **Custom CUDA kernel** (`gpumd_python_kernels.cu`) — adds the JAX-computed AOS-format bias directly to GPUMD's SOA `force_per_atom` in a single kernel launch.
4. **PySAGES backend** (`gpumd.py`) — reconstructs the `Snapshot` from DLPack every step, caches constant data, and applies the computed bias via the custom kernel.
